prompt: Ross's paradox in deontic logic arises from:
options: O(p) implying O(p ∨ q) for any q
Conflicting duties to help and not to interfere
A clash between law and morals
hint: Ross's example: you ought to mail the letter. Must you then mail it or burn it?
explanation: In standard deontic logic O(p) implies O(p ∨ q). So 'you ought to mail the letter' implies 'you ought to mail the letter or burn it', which sounds wrong.
visual_concept: Obligation seems to 'spread' illogically: O(help) → O(help ∨ rob). But surely you're not obligated to 'help or rob'!
